style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Okay, let's sum up all the types of charts and tables. How to read each one, and its trap.
A table: cross a row and a column to find a value. It holds a lot of data, so focus only on what you need.
The trap: in percent questions, know who the whole is. That's what comes after "of". And remember, any problem type, averages, overlap, can hide inside.
Points on axes: each series has its marker in the key, and every point sits exactly at its value. Check the units.
The trap: thousands on the axis. So thirty means thirty thousand. And a zigzag, a Z, means that part of the axis isn't to scale.
A line graph: the values are only at the marked points. The line shows the trend, so steeper means a bigger change.
The trap: reading a value between two points. There's no twenty twelve and a half.
A bar chart: the height is the value. Bars can stand side by side, one inside another, stacked, or lie horizontally... just turn the page.
The trap: in stacked bars, a part is the gap. So commercial vehicles in twenty eleven are twenty-five, not eighty.
A continuous line: every point on it is a measurement. Compare the slopes with your eyes.
The trap: calculating everything. For the biggest relative increase, look for the sharpest slope first.
A range chart: the bottom of the bar is the minimum, the top is the maximum, and the bold line is the mean.
The trap: the mean isn't necessarily the middle. And for "what can't it be", check the extreme cases. Max minus min, and min minus max.
A regions chart: find the point from both axes, and read the number of the area it falls in.
The trap: the units. Ten is ten thousand. So always check against the example.
A circle chart: well, it's a coordinate system bent into a circle. The circles are the value lines, and the hours go round.
The trap: the dark area shows where most visitors are. Not all. So sometimes the answer is, it can't be known.
A cumulative graph: each point is the total so far. So one month is this point minus the previous one.
The trap: reading March's point, fifty, as March's income. March alone is fifty minus twenty, just thirty. Flat means zero that month. And the last point is the grand total.
A change graph: each point is the change from the previous period. Zero means no change.
The trap: the line. Down can be a rise, and flat can be a rise. So ignore it, and look only at the points.
And before every chart set, always do this.
Read the explanation, and check the example in the chart. Does it match what you understand?
Look at the titles, the units, thousands, percent, and every note.
The questions get harder as you go. The first one usually just pulls out a value.
And if the example still isn't clear after a slow second reading, skip the set and come back at the end. But a chart at the start of the section... don't skip it. Good luck.
